title: Nicholas Nickleby
full_review:
The comforting tale of a young man's triumph over adversity in 19th-century England is handsomely realized in writer-director Douglas McGrath's adaptation of the Charles Dickens classic, "Nicholas Nickleby" (MGM).

Pared down from the immense 1839 novel and the nine-hour Royal Shakespeare Company stage production, the movie still charms with its almost-too-good-to-be-true title hero (Charlie Hunnam) at the mercy of a cold and calculating uncle (Christopher Plummer).

A gentle opening, encapsulating how Nicholas and then Kate (Romola Garal) were born and tenderly raised by loving parents gives way to their father's death and their penniless arrival with their mother (Stella Gonet) at the doorstep of Uncle Ralph. He quickly dispatches Kate to work with a dressmaker and delivers 19-year-old Nicholas into the evil hands of grasping Wackford Squeers (Jim Broadbent) to work as a teacher in Squeers' distant, prison-like academy. There Nicholas befriends crippled adolescent Smike (Jamie Bell), whom sadistic Squeers and his equally rotten spouse (Juliet Stevenson) have held as a slave ever since his tuition payments ceased seven years earlier.

Appalled at the vicious treatment the Squeerses dole out to one and all, Nicholas escapes with Smike, determined to reunite with his family and somehow provide for them all. Along the way, he is pleasantly waylaid by traveling performers (led by Nathan Lane) and cajoled into starring as Romeo before he and Smike arrive in London and learn of his uncle's callous mistreatment of Kate.

Although he finds work and meets the lovely Madeline (Anne Hathaway), once again his uncle intervenes, deliberately setting in motion an arranged marriage for Madeline to the craven Sir Mulberry Hawk (Edward Fox). Even as Smike's health fails, the uncle's disgruntled servant (Tom Courtenay) aligns with Nicholas to bring a halt to his employer's lifetime of greed-fueled misdeeds.

Consummate storyteller Dickens' concern for the human condition and especially the poor shines through in this heart-warming adaptation. Of necessity, filmmaker McGrath has compressed the tale and eliminated characters, but those who remain bring their roles to vivid life. Alternately thundering then whispering, the crafty Plummer steals the show and invests his comeuppance with sudden unexpected gravitas. But nearly as riveting are Courtenay as his insolent, alcoholic servant, Broadbent as the steely, one-eyed monster and Stevenson as his witch of a wife.

At the other end of the emotional scale, Lane and Alan Cumming as the performer with a yen to dance the Highland Fling provide much-needed whimsy during Nicholas' arduous journey to manhood. Hunnam in the title role delivers considerable eye appeal, but doesn't yet have the acting chops of the other featured performers. Nor is his romance with underused love interest Hathaway sufficiently fleshed out.

The accomplished production design conveys the horrors of the ghastly boarding school and is most effective at showing how Uncle Ralph's rich but bleak home, with its collection of stuffed animals, is a house empty of life or love.

With its attention to the mistreatment of children and themes of family, friendship and perseverance, "Nicholas Nickleby" is rewarding, high-minded fare.

Because of brief violence, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-II -- adults and adolescents. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG -- parental guidance suggested.
